title: WhatsApp Voice-Note Superintendent for Spec Builders
one_liner: A bilingual coordinator-plus-AI service that runs daily crew confirmations, headcounts and re-sequencing for a builder's two dozen subs over WhatsApp voice notes, priced per house.
customer: Small private and spec builders (20-300 homes a year) in Texas, Florida and the Southeast, and remodelers who juggle many subs.
problem: A typical home needs about two dozen subs. Foundations sit 30+ days waiting for crews, and one executive described 15-20 houses stuck 6+ weeks. Builders learn a crew is not coming days too late. Project software requires English typing and logins, and workers are wary of anything that looks like tracking. Procore's 20 agents serve larger GCs.
solution: Foremen keep sending Spanish voice notes on WhatsApp. The system transcribes them, extracts headcount, phase status and photos, and updates the schedule. A nearshore bilingual coordinator confirms tomorrow's crews by 5 p.m., calls backup crews when there is a gap, and sends the builder one exception report each morning. Privacy by design: counts and progress only, no IDs or location.
why_now: ICE arrests rose from 32,545 in May to 49,571 in July 2026. Crews can shrink overnight (a Minnesota roofing crew went from 80 to 6). Multilingual speech models and the WhatsApp Business API are mature, and PM incumbents are focused on big GCs.
revenue_model: $300-500 per active house per month, or $3-6K per month per builder. One coordinator handles 25-40 houses, so gross margin is high.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not scheduling math, it is that the people who know whether tomorrow's crew is coming do not use the software. The interface must be the phone and language they already use. The daily headcount is the leading indicator, and knowing a day earlier lets a builder re-sequence trades instead of idling a foundation.
first_30_days: Sign 3 builders with 10-20 active houses each through a home builders association. Hire one bilingual coordinator. Run it manually with WhatsApp and a shared sheet, add speech-to-text in week 2, and document five saved crew-days.

title: Indonesia Halal Rescue for Food Exporters
one_liner: A fast-track service that gets mid-size food, supplement and cosmetics exporters registered and documented under Indonesia's mandatory halal regime, then keeps them compliant.
customer: Mid-size US, EU and Australian exporters and their Indonesian importers, plus halal certifiers who white-label the work.
problem: Halal certification becomes mandatory for imported food, beverages, cosmetics and supplements on 17 Oct 2026, with enforcement from 18 Oct. The authority says no extensions, certification takes 3-6 months, and USDA FAS (Sept 2026) flags roughly $2.5B of US ag exports affected. Many mid-size firms treat halal as a marketing label and have not started.
solution: A gap analysis, supplier halal-declaration collection, matching to recognized foreign halal bodies, registration filing, and label and claim review. A software ledger tracks every ingredient and supplier certificate across SKUs and alerts on expiry, which also serves kosher and EU documentation needs.
why_now: The cliff is three weeks away and the lead time exceeds that, so late movers face shipment holds. After the deadline the work shifts to cure (relabeling, re-filing, clearing stuck shipments), which is recurring.
revenue_model: $4-15k per SKU-family project plus $500-2k/month monitoring, and certifier white-label fees.
non_obvious_insight: Halal has become a customs gate rather than a marketing certificate, so budgets come from logistics and compliance, not brand. The ingredient-and-supplier documentation ledger is reusable across regimes.
first_30_days: Email and LinkedIn outreach to 300 exporters from USDA export directories and state trade offices, offering a $750 48-hour readiness check. Partner with 1-2 recognized halal bodies and prioritize firms with shipments already in transit.

title: Technique Capture for Cell Therapy Tech Transfer
one_liner: Instrumented video-and-sensor capture of the 'artisanal' manual steps in cell therapy processes, turned into numeric parameters and training packages for CDMO tech transfer.
customer: Cell and gene therapy developers moving from academic or pilot scale to a CDMO, CDMO MSAT teams, and automation vendors as secondary buyers.
problem: Roughly 10% of a ~5,000-action biomanufacturing workflow is manual and resists automation, for example cell resuspension. The know-how sits in one technician's hands. As cell therapies scale and CDMOs cut staff, process know-how is getting lost in tech transfer. Failed transfers burn months and millions. Cellares' 168 layoffs after BMS ended the partnership show automation capex is fragile.
solution: A 'Technique Package': multi-angle video with hand and pose tracking, Bluetooth pipettes and force or flow sensors, timing, and cell-state images at each critical manual step. Convert it into acceptable ranges, failure signatures, operator training clips and a comparability protocol, delivered before CDMO engineering runs. With customer consent, the data doubles as a physical-AI training set.
why_now: The 5,000-action and 10% artisanal figures come from 2026 GEN reporting. CDMO staff cuts are eroding institutional knowledge. Cheap wearables and egocentric-video models are mature. Transfyr's $25M seed proves investor appetite for the underlying data but targets a different buyer.
revenue_model: $25-120k per transfer package, per-operator training licenses, and data licensing with revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: Sold as tech-transfer insurance (avoid failed engineering runs), not as automation. It needs no robot, no capex and no bet on which automation vendor survives. Buyers pay from the transfer budget, which is already allocated.
first_30_days: Build the kit from off-the-shelf parts. Offer two CGT startups planning CDMO transfers a $20-25k pilot. Capture three high-variance steps and document before-and-after run success.

title: Clinician-Prescribed AI Social Practice for Kids
one_liner: A bounded, transcript-visible role-play partner that speech-language pathologists prescribe to autistic and socially anxious kids, sold to districts that are legally obliged to deliver therapy minutes.
customer: School-district special-education departments, contract therapy staffing firms (SLP, psychology) and private pediatric therapy clinics.
problem: Insiders think kids plus AI is a no-go zone. Character.AI barred under-18s from open-ended chat in November 2025, and the FTC 6(b) inquiry and state laws (CA SB 243) followed. But districts must deliver IEP speech and social-communication minutes, SLP caseloads are huge and vacancies persist. Kids need many low-stakes repetitions between weekly 30-minute sessions.
solution: An anti-companion design: the SLP assigns scripted scenarios (ordering lunch, joining a game, handling teasing). There is no persona, no persistent memory and no free topics. Practice is recorded and the SLP dashboard produces the progress-monitoring data IEPs require. Parents can read transcripts. Voice-first, tuned for child speech, with no audio retention by default.
why_now: Regulators and lawsuits (Raine v. OpenAI, Pennsylvania v. Character.AI) closed the open-ended companion door, which makes scoped, clinician-in-the-loop tools the defensible lane. Speech models handle child speech far better than they did two years ago. Special-ed budgets are stretched (from memory).
revenue_model: Per-student annual licence ($150-400), much cheaper than added SLP hours at $60-100 an hour. Clinics pay per clinician seat.
non_obvious_insight: The regulated lane isn't closed, it just has a different buyer: a clinician with a legal duty to document. Designing it as the opposite of a companion (no persona, no memory, no free chat) makes it compliant by construction and defensible in the next lawsuit.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 practicing SLPs to script 30 scenarios. Build a voice prototype. Run a 4-week paid pilot with about 10 kids in one private clinic ($99 a month per child). Then approach one contract-therapy staffing firm with the pilot's progress-monitoring data.

title: Proctored Truth Audits for School Edtech
one_liner: Short, paper-based, device-free probes that tell districts whether the practice software they license teaches anything, now that AI can do the practice for the child.
customer: District curriculum and assessment directors (5k-50k student districts) that renew six-figure math/ELA practice licenses; secondary: charter networks. Edtech vendors are a later, firewalled buyer of verified listings.
problem: Practice dashboards show rising accuracy, but ALEKS data (June 2026 working paper, not peer-reviewed) show proctored word-problem accuracy falling from about 80% to about 60% after ChatGPT while unsupervised accuracy rose. A 2-year Tennessee study found Khanmigo added nothing over Khan Academy alone. Districts renew on usage and mastery metrics that AI now contaminates.
solution: Twenty-minute proctored paper probes at the start, middle and end of term, on a random sample of classrooms, aligned to the same standards as the platform and including graphing items that are hard to paste into AI. Human-scored from scans. Output is a per-product, per-school report: what share of platform 'mastery' survives an unassisted check, and cost per verified mastery. Later, a benchmark vendors pay to be listed on.
why_now: Unsupervised practice data has visibly decoupled from learning (2026 ALEKS study). ESSER money is gone, so renewals get scrutiny. NYC and LAUSD paused AI for 2026-27, and boards now want proof. Over half of teachers say AI harms critical thinking.
revenue_model: Annual district audit contracts of $15k-60k per product per grade band, plus per-school scanning and scoring fees. Later, vendor-funded verification listings kept separate from the audit results.
non_obvious_insight: When students can outsource practice, engagement and accuracy metrics measure the AI, not the child. The only trustworthy learning data is now scarce, unassisted and physical, so the measurement layer, not the content layer, becomes the moat.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 curriculum directors who are mid-renewal fight. Run a free 6-classroom pilot with paper probes built from released state-test items plus hand-drawn graphing items. Have a few retired teachers score them. Hand over a 2-page usage-versus-learning report before their renewal decision, then convert to a $15-25k paid audit.

title: Heat-Health Desk for Medicare Advantage Plans
one_liner: Forecast-triggered outreach and cooling delivery for the heat-vulnerable members whose hospital bills the health plan pays.
customer: Medicare Advantage, D-SNP and Medicaid managed-care plans in the Southwest, Southeast and Pacific Northwest (supplemental-benefits and medical-director teams).
problem: Summer 2026 brought the hottest US July on record and a European heatwave with about 38,000 provisional deaths (secondary source). Heat waves drive ER visits and admissions among older, medicated, low-income members. Plans pay the downstream cost but do not know which members lack working cooling or live on top floors. Cooling supplemental benefits are underused.
solution: Risk-stratify members by housing type, utility arrears, medications that impair heat tolerance and prior heat visits. Trigger phone outreach ahead of forecast heat, deliver and install AC or fans through partners, run check-in calls on days 1-3, and help prevent utility shutoffs. Report avoided ER visits.
why_now: After the 2026 heat shock, plan medical directors are looking for concrete heat programs. Off-season (Oct-Feb) is when supplemental-benefit budgets get set.
revenue_model: Per targeted member per month in season, or per intervention, plus shared savings.
non_obvious_insight: The party that absorbs the cost of heat is the health plan, not the city. Heat is a claims-management problem and belongs in the plan's budget.
first_30_days: Use public hospital heat-visit data to build a cost-per-heat-day case. Pitch 5 regional plans for a 2,000-member pilot next season, and line up an AC-delivery and check-in vendor.

title: Second-opinion technical review for city data center deals
one_liner: A fixed-fee package for small cities facing a data center: adversarial review of the developer's noise, water and power submissions, plus a term sheet built from the few community benefit agreements that exist.
customer: Planning directors, city managers and county administrators in jurisdictions under a data center moratorium or first inquiry, mostly populations of 5k-150k that cannot afford a big-firm consultant. They pay $8k-25k per package, and the cost can often be recovered from the applicant through an escrow for third-party review.
problem: Small governments are negotiating blind against developers' consultants. Broken Arrow, OK issued an RFQ for consultants to 'advise on environmental, water, noise, utilities and fiscal modeling' and needs recommendations by year-end 2026 or a moratorium extension. Fort Worth voted unanimously for a moratorium, Chicago introduced one in September 2026, and Lexington, KY paused approvals until at least Oct 31, 2026. NPR reports that deals such as the one in Boyce, Louisiana were negotiated under NDAs. The Federation of American Scientists found only eight executed community benefit agreements, only one fully executed and publicly posted (Lancaster, PA), and says 'best practices are not readily available'.
solution: A productized package. (1) An ordinance with fill-in standards: setbacks, dBA limits at the property line, closed-loop or reclaimed-water requirements, decommissioning bond, and utility-capacity verification. (2) A fiscal calculator comparing abatement to service and infrastructure costs, plus water/wastewater and power-interconnection checks. (3) A term-sheet library annotated from the known executed CBAs. (4) A retained on-call review of the developer's noise study, water plan and load forecast by contract engineers, with a plain-language memo the council can read in open session. Moratorium end dates are natural deadlines that pull purchases forward.
why_now: Data center siting became the top local land-use fight of 2026: Wixom MI, Denver, Fort Worth, San Antonio, Lexington, Broken Arrow and Chicago all acted this year, and more cities keep opening moratorium clocks. Developer NDAs are now a political issue, which pushes officials to buy independent review.
revenue_model: $8k-25k fixed fee per package; $2.5k/month retainer during active negotiation; per-review fee for developer-funded escrow; a subscription comparables database (abatement terms, water allocations, decommissioning bonds) for state municipal leagues.
non_obvious_insight: Ordinance templates are free and cities can copy them; the scarce thing is an adversarial reader of the developer's technical submissions, because the city's only counterpart is the developer's own consultants under NDA. Applicant-funded escrow lets the city avoid a budget fight, so procurement is quick. Evidence: Broken Arrow's RFQ scope and year-end deadline (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9481196/oklahoma/tulsa-county/broken-arrow/city-council-meetings/city-forms-datacenter-study-committee-says-ordinance-moratorium-remains-in-place); the gap in best practices and only eight executed CBAs (https://fas.org/publication/data-center-community-benefit-agreements/); NDA-shrouded deals (https://www.npr.org/2026/08/27/nx-s1-5879528/data-center-nda-disclosure-louisiana); Fort Worth's unanimous moratorium (https://fortworthreport.org/2026/08/12/data-center-moratorium-takes-first-steps-after-fort-worth-city-councils-unanimous-vote/).
first_30_days: Publish a free comparison of the eight known CBAs and a one-page 'questions to ask a data center developer' for planning directors. Email 30 planning directors in cities with moratoria expiring in the next 6 months. Line up 2 retired utility or acoustic engineers as contract reviewers. Sell 2 fixed-fee review memos at $6k each, ideally funded by the applicant's escrow.

title: Orphaned Job and Membership Rescue Desk
one_liner: When a PE roll-up of contractors collapses, package its unfinished jobs, prepaid maintenance memberships and warranties and hand them to healthy local contractors, while lenders and trustees get paid for the recovery.
customer: Two payers. (1) Private-credit lenders, Chapter 11 trustees and creditor committees of collapsed home-service platforms, on a success fee. (2) Local independent contractors and newly formed tech-owned shops, who pay a per-customer transfer fee to inherit service obligations and customer relationships.
problem: Roll-ups of HVAC, remodeling and roofing firms are failing, and the stranded parties have no one to coordinate. Homeowners are left with half-finished jobs and prepaid plans. Laid-off technicians hold the customer relationships but not the customer data. Lenders are owed $100M+ from shells with almost no assets and have no operating capability to finish jobs and collect receivables.
solution: A rapid-response playbook plus lightweight software: (1) an intake site for stranded customers ('my contractor shut down'); (2) an import of the estate's job, warranty and membership data from its field-service or CRM exports, scored by job stage, deposit status, and geography; (3) matching to vetted local contractors, with milestone escrow so the deposit follows the work; (4) a lender/trustee dashboard showing completed WIP and recovered receivables. A starter kit (entity formation, insurance, licensing checklist, FSM software setup) lets laid-off technicians become buyers of the books they used to serve.
why_now: 2025 was a record year for PE-linked distress. The PE Stakeholder Project counts PE firms in 19 of the 35 largest US bankruptcies (54%) and 21 of 41 large ones (51%) in 2025, though it is an advocacy source. Bain's 2026 reports say borrowing costs are 8-9% versus 6-7% a decade ago, and deals now need 10-12% annual EBITDA growth to hit target returns. That squeezes leveraged service roll-ups. Private credit, not banks, now holds much of the paper, and these lenders lack turnaround operations for field-service businesses.
revenue_model: 5-10% success fee on WIP completed and receivables recovered for the estate. $150-400 per customer transferred, paid by the acquiring contractor. Optional 1-1.5% escrow fee on consumer deposits. Subscription for lenders who want a watchlist and pre-built playbook.
non_obvious_insight: In a roll-up collapse the valuable asset is the unfulfilled service obligations (prepaid memberships, warranties, half-built jobs), not the brand or customer list. Local independents will pay to inherit them, and lenders recover more from orderly completion than from a liquidation. Renovo, formed in 2021 by Audax by combining three home-remodeling businesses (later seven), filed in November 2025 with about $50,000 in assets against more than $100M in liabilities, after roughly $150M from BlackRock, Apollo and Oaktree. About 1,500 workers were terminated, some without final paychecks, and homeowners were left with incomplete projects. Cutting installer pay from 10-12% to 8% drove out skilled workers (https://pestakeholder.org/private-equity-bankruptcy-tracker/). In September 2026 PE-backed United Air Temp (Littlejohn's United Comfort Group, eight partner companies) filed WARN notices for 135+ layoffs across VA and MD, closing its Lorton HQ effective Nov 10, 2026 (https://www.achrnews.com/articles/166687-private-equity-backed-united-air-temp-announces-mass-layoffs). WARN notices are a free, public lead source for the next rescue.
first_30_days: Build a watchlist from public WARN notices and bankruptcy dockets for home-service platforms. Stand up a 'my contractor shut down' landing page and intake form for one distressed metro. Sign 5 local independent contractors who agree to take transferred customers at a flat fee. Cold-approach restructuring counsel and Chapter 11 trustees at 5-10 private-credit special-situations desks with a free 2-week pilot on a small estate. Estate authority over customer data will be the gating legal step, so line up a bankruptcy attorney early.

title: Data Act Broker for Equipment Owners
one_liner: File and operationalize EU Data Act data-access demands so independent service shops can finally read the diagnostics that elevator, heat-pump, forklift and tractor makers lock away.
customer: Independent maintenance and service companies in the EU (starting with elevator/escalator maintainers, then commercial heat-pump installers, forklift and ag-machinery shops). They pay per monitored asset per month. Equipment-owning businesses (building managers, hospitals, logistics sites) are the secondary payer, because they hold the legal right.
problem: Original manufacturers use exclusive access to machine diagnostics and fault logs to keep 60-80% of the lucrative service market. Independents work blind, so they lose contracts to OEMs. The EU Data Act (applicable since 12 Sep 2025) gives the user of a connected product, including a business, the right to get the data the product generates. The user can also have it handed to any third party of their choice. In practice almost nobody exercises the right. The paperwork is unfamiliar, OEMs stall, and the data arrives in a different format from every vendor.
solution: An agency-plus-plumbing service. (1) Sign a user-authorization letter with the equipment owner. (2) Auto-generate and file the Article 4/5 access and third-party-sharing requests to each OEM and track statutory response deadlines. (3) Ingest whatever comes back, whether an API, a file dump or a portal export. (4) Normalize it into one cross-vendor schema per asset class. (5) Give the independent shop a fleet-health dashboard and fault-prediction alerts. Add a public compliance scorecard showing which OEMs comply, and escalate the ones that do not to national enforcement authorities.
why_now: The Data Act became applicable on 12 Sep 2025. On 12 Sep 2026, 16 days ago, its design obligation started applying to newly placed connected products, so data must be accessible by default. The right-to-repair movement is at peak momentum. OEM stonewalling now generates complaints that regulators must act on. No one has industrialized user-side requests yet, so the first mover sets the standard schema and templates.
revenue_model: Setup fee of about 50-150 EUR per asset for the request and integration work, plus 4-12 EUR per asset per month for the normalized feed and health analytics. Add-ons: predictive-maintenance alerts and a white-label owner portal. Later: sell anonymized cross-fleet reliability benchmarks to insurers and asset owners.
non_obvious_insight: A legal right is worthless until someone industrializes exercising it. The Data Act gives the data-access key to the owner, not the repairer, so the winning business acts as the owner's agent and sells the result to the repairer. The moat is accumulated request templates, OEM-by-OEM response knowledge, and one normalized schema. Every OEM refusal also becomes evidence for regulators, which turns compliance friction into marketing.
first_30_days: Pick one vertical and one country pair, for example independent elevator maintainers in Germany and the Netherlands, and reach them through trade associations. Retain a Data Act lawyer for a fixed fee to finalize request templates. Recruit 5 independent shops, get user-authorization letters covering about 50 units, and file the requests. Log every OEM response and format. Charge a pilot fee of about 1-2k EUR per shop for delivered data plus a first fleet report. Publish an OEM response-time tracker to build inbound demand. Expect uneven enforcement, so keep the pilot to OEMs that respond and use the ones that stonewall as regulator evidence.

title: Peptide Assurance Mark for Clinics and Processors
one_liner: Independent lot testing and supplier audit with a QR-verifiable mark that lets peptide sellers pass payment-processor and insurer underwriting.
customer: 503A compounding pharmacies, peptide and longevity clinic chains, and the payment processors and insurers who need evidence to underwrite them.
problem: HHS moved ~14 of 19 Category 2 peptides (BPC-157, TB-500, GHK-Cu and others) back toward compoundable in Feb 2026, and an FDA panel backed BPC-157 and KPV on Jul 23. Clinics are multiplying, but Stripe and card networks exclude the category and Forbes (Jun 30, 2026) called it a '$1 billion industry banks won't touch'. Losing a merchant account kills sellers faster than FDA action.
solution: ISO 17025 lab partners test identity, purity, endotoxin, sterility and potency per lot. Supplier and chain-of-custody audits feed a public registry and QR verification that processors, insurers and state boards can accept, with annual certification and monitoring.
why_now: The legal window opened in 2026 with no infrastructure. Purity is uneven, and processors need third-party evidence to underwrite certified merchants.
revenue_model: $250-600 per lot test, $5-15k/year certification, and processor referral fees for certified merchants.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is payments and insurance, not FDA. A credible independent mark is the key that unlocks mainstream merchant accounts, so processors are the hidden buyer.
first_30_days: Contract an accredited lab and run a blind-purchase audit of 30 popular BPC-157 and GHK-Cu products, published as a report. Sell $500 audits to 10 clinics and approach two high-risk processors about fast-tracking certified merchants.

title: Asset-Light Black Mass Desk Under BIS Rule
one_liner: A trading and compliance desk that becomes the default outlet for US black mass sellers, using the rule's toll-processing exception instead of building plants.
customer: Scrap managers at US cell gigafactories and black-mass aggregators (sellers), who pay brokerage and compliance fees. Toll processors with idle hydromet capacity pay for feed access.
problem: Since the Aug 27, 2026 BIS/DPA rule, sellers must allocate 100% of monthly black mass sales to US buyers. Domestic buyers are thin after Ascend's Chapter 11 and Li-Cycle's bankruptcy, and DOE grants were cancelled. Sellers face legal exposure, a one-sided bid, and assay disputes. BIS has said more materials may be added.
solution: A desk that (1) certifies sampling and assay per lot, (2) documents and allocates monthly volumes across US buyers, (3) structures toll-processing corridors. These run through domestic hydromet capacity, or through foreign processors whose intermediates return to the US, which the rule exempts. (4) It issues a per-lot compliance file. It never owns a plant, only feedstock relationships and the legal wrapper.
why_now: The BIS temporary final rule (Aug 2026) makes domestic allocation mandatory and toll-processing the only export route. Manufacturing scrap is about two-thirds of North American battery feedstock through 2030, so the flow is real. Capex-heavy players have just failed.
revenue_model: 2-4% brokerage on lot value, $1-3K per-lot assay and compliance-file fee, toll-margin on structured deals, and a monthly subscription for allocation reporting.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders read Ascend and Li-Cycle as proof that battery recycling does not work. They actually proved that owning capex ahead of feedstock timing does not work. The BIS rule turned feedstock rights plus a legal wrapper into the scarce asset, and the money sits between captive sellers and stranded capacity.
first_30_days: Read the rule with a trade lawyer and publish a 6-page 'what this means for sellers' note. Cold-call scrap managers at cell plants and the top 10 aggregators. Sign 2-3 non-exclusive brokerage LOIs. Collect toll price sheets from 2 US processors and 1 Asian or European processor. Target the first structured lot in about 90 days.

title: Rent Ledger for Adult Kids Living at Home
one_liner: A simple lease, payment and credit-reporting layer that lets parents charge their adult children rent, build the kids' credit history, and quietly bank the money as a down-payment fund.
customer: Parents (Gen X and Boomers) with adult children aged 22-30 living at home, paying $12/month per household. Secondary revenue from mortgage lenders and first-time-buyer programs.
problem: Nearly half (49%) of US adults under 30 lived with parents in 2025, up 12 percentage points from 2019 (Federal Reserve SHED). Only 63% of adults could cover a $400 emergency with cash or a paid-off card, and the Fed reports 16% of adults use buy-now-pay-later, with 11% of users hit by overdraft fees from missed payments. Lender-side data shows BNPL is spreading into groceries (a LendingTree survey reported nearly a quarter of BNPL users financed groceries, up from 14%; 41% reported a late payment). These young adults are paying for hobbies, subscriptions and installment plans while accruing no rent history at all, since informal family housing builds no credit and no savings discipline.
solution: An app that produces a simple parent-child lease, collects a modest monthly 'rent' by ACH, reports on-time payments to the credit bureaus through an established rent-reporting partner (do not become a furnisher), and lets the parent choose to escrow the money in a labeled account toward a future down payment or move-out fund. It gives the kid a monthly statement and a BNPL and subscription view so obligations don't collide with rent day. It includes parent-side documentation of the rent for tax purposes (tax treatment is a gray area, so it needs CPA-reviewed templates).
why_now: The 12-point jump in under-30s living at home is now structural, not a pandemic blip. Rent reporting has been mainstreamed by consumer fintechs and by underwriting systems that count rental payment history, and BNPL late payments are rising, which raises the value of a credibility-building habit. Housing costs make first-time down payments the main goal for these households.
revenue_model: $12/month per household (parent pays), $5/month optional kid add-on for credit-builder features. Referral fees from mortgage lenders and down-payment-assistance programs when the kid buys. Later: employer benefit channel for parents.
non_obvious_insight: Parents are the largest unpriced landlord class in the US, and they already hold the leverage the market lacks: the kid will pay them and will not skip. The product isn't a rent app, it is a behavioral bridge that converts a free-rent arrangement into credit history plus parent-held savings. Evidence: Federal Reserve SHED 2025 https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2026-economic-well-being-of-us-households-in-2025-executive-summary.htm (49% of under-30s living with parents, +12 points since 2019; 63% cover $400; 16% BNPL, 11% overdraft fees) and BNPL grocery and late-payment figures via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buy_now,_pay_later (summarizing LendingTree). Assumptions to validate first: that bureaus and lenders will accept rent reported for a parent-landlord and how underwriting treats it, and that parents want to charge rent and save it. I found no survey on either.
first_30_days: Interview 20 parents in local parenting and finance Facebook groups. Test a landing page and a $12/month waitlist. Run a concierge pilot with 10 families: a lease template, ACH collection, an existing rent-reporting partner and a shared spreadsheet. Confirm with a mortgage broker whether reported parent-landlord rent helps underwriting. Target 15 paying families and one lender-partner conversation.

title: One Annual Fee for Every Mandatory EU Representative
one_liner: A roll-up of small EU authorised-representative shops that bundles every legally required local presence (GDPR Art. 27, AI Act, Data Act, product safety, CRA) into one liability-bearing annual contract for non-EU companies.
customer: US, UK, Israeli, Indian and Asian SaaS, AI and hardware companies ($2M-$200M revenue) selling in the EU without an EU entity. Bought by founders, GCs and ops leads.
problem: Several EU regimes require non-EU companies to name someone in the EU who can be held to account: GDPR Art. 27, AI Act authorised representatives for high-risk and GPAI providers, Data Act legal representative, product-safety responsible person, an optional CRA authorised representative (background knowledge; verify each). Today each comes from a different vendor, many are one-person shops or law firms wary of liability, and none coordinate.
solution: Acquire three to six small rep businesses (typically hundreds to a couple thousand clients on sticky annual fees), keep their brands, and rebuild operations with automation for inbound regulator and data-subject mail triage, translation and escalation. Add an EU law-firm panel as backstop and sell one bundle with a shared register of representations, one invoice and standard playbooks, priced for the liability.
why_now: GPAI duties applied Aug 2025 with enforcement from Aug 2026, Data Act obligations arrived Sep 2025 and Sep 2026, and CRA reporting started 11 Sep 2026, so many non-EU firms suddenly face three or four rep obligations at once. AI lowers the cost of delivering the service.
revenue_model: EUR 3-15k/year per client bundle, 70-80% renewal, acquisitions at roughly 1-2x revenue, and upsell to compliance retainers.
non_obvious_insight: When AI makes drafting free, the scarce good is someone in the EU who can be sued. Liability-bearing presence has pricing power and stickiness, and becoming the address regulators write to is a distribution moat.
first_30_days: List 30 small EU rep providers and approach five owners about a white-label or revenue-share deal that leads to acquisition. Sell the bundle to 10 US SaaS and AI firms through founder communities at EUR 4k and obtain a professional-indemnity quote.

title: Pay Farmers to Under-Irrigate, Not Fallow
one_liner: A broker and satellite-verification layer that pays growers of alfalfa, hay and cotton for mid-season deficit irrigation and hands corporate and municipal buyers audited acre-feet.
customer: Buyers: corporate water coalitions (Amazon put $20M into the Water Resilience Coalition's Colorado River effort, $32M raised toward a $100M goal) and Lower Basin cities and water agencies. Sellers: irrigation districts and forage/annual-crop growers. The buyer pays.
problem: The 2027-2036 Colorado River framework pushes cuts onto agriculture (about 70% of the river), yet corporate money has no settlement layer. Fallowing is politically toxic and guts farm income. Drip and efficiency upgrades often do not reduce consumptive use, so nobody can say what a verified acre-foot is.
solution: A standard split-season contract. The grower skips the last irrigation cycles, or accepts deficit irrigation at pre-agreed growth stages. Consumptive use is measured by satellite ET (an OpenET-style ensemble) against a five-year baseline and paired control fields. Payment is escrowed per verified acre-foot, and the buyer gets a basin-and-year-tagged certificate. Wedge product: one district pilot plus a buyer dashboard. Federal credit is not needed to start, so begin with districts that already hold Reclamation conservation agreements.
why_now: The Aug 2026 Record of Decision fixed the 2027-2036 rules. Powell plus Mead storage is about 36% of capacity, the lowest since before Glen Canyon Dam filled. Corporate money is arriving, and open ET datasets are now good enough to audit individual fields.
revenue_model: 10-15% spread on each acre-foot transaction (roughly $40-90 on a $400-600/af price), plus $20-50k/yr verification SaaS to districts.
non_obvious_insight: Only cuts in consumptive use create basin-level savings, and forage crops tolerate a mid-season deficit far better than farm economies tolerate fallowed fields. Buyers are really paying for measurement certainty, so whoever owns the audit trail sets the price and the standard.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: run retrospective ET for 10 alfalfa/hay growers in one Lower Basin or Grand Valley district (public data, free tier) and price the acre-feet they could offer. Days 10-25: build a one-page buyer pitch and dashboard mock. Days 25-30: pitch the Water Resilience Coalition and two city water agencies to underwrite a 500-1,000 af pilot for the 2027 season, since contracts get negotiated over winter.

title: Compliance Co-op for Group-Buy Hobby Hardware
angle: Pairing 1: Legal services, compliance & new regulations (EU AI Act, privacy, PFAS, right to repair, etc.) x Weird, niche and overlooked markets (hobbies, collectibles, faith communities, subcultures)
one_liner: A pooled EU compliance desk (CRA incident reporting, EU responsible person, battery/e-waste registrations, SBOM monitoring) that lets one-person keyboard, FPV, synth and LoRa hardware makers keep selling to Europe.
customer: Boutique hardware makers of 1-20 people in enthusiast scenes: custom mechanical keyboards, eurorack/synth modules, FPV drone boards, LoRa/Meshtastic radios, 3D-printer upgrade kits. They sell through group buys, Tindie, Kickstarter and Discord shops, including US and Asian makers shipping into the EU/UK, plus the boutique vendors that resell them.
problem: Per the briefing, the EU Cyber Resilience Act's 24-hour vulnerability/incident reporting duty went live 11 Sep 2026 for products with digital elements, Data Act connected-product design duties began 12 Sep 2026, and full CRA conformity is due 11 Dec 2027 (fines up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover). Those duties fall on whoever sells the product, and in hobby scenes that is a hobbyist selling a 300-unit run built on open-source firmware (QMK, Betaflight, Klipper, Meshtastic). The CRA's open-source carve-out protects non-commercial projects, not the person selling hardware with the firmware. Stack on the EU General Product Safety Regulation's EU-responsible-person requirement (in force since Dec 2024), radio-equipment cybersecurity rules, and battery and WEEE registrations (battery labelling duties start around Aug 2026, verify), and the makers' choices are to ignore it or stop shipping to the EU. A EUR 5-10k consultancy engagement is impossible on an $80-300 product.
solution: A membership 'compliance-of-record' co-op. Members get: a named EU responsible person and CRA contact of record (professional-indemnity insured); a shared coordinated-vulnerability-disclosure desk with a tested runbook for filing on ENISA's single reporting platform within 24 hours; a CI plug-in that generates SBOMs and watches firmware dependencies (QMK, ChibiOS, ESP-IDF, Zephyr etc.) for exploited CVEs; declaration-of-conformity and technical-file templates by product class; a battery/EPR registration bundle; and a group-buy contract addendum covering delivery windows and customised-goods withdrawal rights. The co-op also acts as liaison to upstream open-source firmware projects and channels 'sponsored security fixes' to them.
why_now: CRA reporting has been live for about 18 days and the Data Act design duties for 17 (per briefing). Market-surveillance sweeps and marketplace delistings typically follow such dates, and marketplaces already delist listings that lack GPSR data. Full conformity lands 11 Dec 2027, so scenes will look for a shared answer during 2026-27, before any vendor has locked the niche.
revenue_model: Annual dues tiered by EU units shipped (about EUR 390/yr up to 500 units, EUR 1,200 up to 5,000, custom above). Per-SKU onboarding fee of EUR 250-750. Optional micro-levy of EUR 0.10-0.25 per unit that funds the incident desk and upstream firmware maintainers. Paid 'CRA sprint' for makers with more than 5 SKUs.
non_obvious_insight: Regulators wrote these rules for companies with a compliance department, but the enthusiast hardware economy is thousands of micro-manufacturers who share the same three failure points: firmware dependencies, 24-hour incident reporting, and an EU address. The scalable unit of compliance is the scene or firmware ecosystem, not the individual maker. A co-op that pools the boring 80% and is trusted inside the scene's Discords beats both a law firm and a generic authorised-representative vendor, because reputation in the scene is the distribution channel.
first_30_days: Pick one scene (custom keyboards on QMK/VIA, or LoRa/Meshtastic). Interview 15 makers from group-buy vendor lists. Have a compliance lawyer and a firmware engineer write a one-page '24-hour CRA reporting runbook' and post it free in the scene's Discords, r/MechanicalKeyboards and Geekhack. Sign 10 founding members at about EUR 250 for year one, deliver an incident-reporting drill and a template technical file for one product class, and sell fixed-price single-SKU audits. Cost is two part-time experts plus a simple site, and break-even is roughly 40 members.

title: Assisted Short Sales for Underwater Auto Loans
one_liner: Record auto originations lead to record delinquencies and a repossession glut. Give lenders a mortgage-style short sale for cars that recovers more than auction does.
customer: Credit unions and subprime and indirect auto lenders with rising 60-plus-day delinquencies.
problem: Auto originations hit a record $211B and auto delinquencies also hit a record (CNBC and others, Aug 2026). Lenders' only tool at scale is repossession and auction, which is slow, costly and yields discounted recoveries. Borrowers keep a deficiency balance and wrecked credit, and lenders lose more than a cooperative sale would cost them.
solution: At 45-60 days delinquent, the lender offers the borrower a lender-blessed voluntary sale. The platform lists the car at retail to dealers and private buyers, handles payoff letters, title and lien release in each state, and converts the shortfall into a small structured note or forgiveness within lender-set limits. The lender pays only when its net recovery beats projected repo loss.
why_now: Delinquencies at records, auction supply pressure, and credit unions with growing delinquent books and a reputation to protect. Mortgage short-sale playbooks are well understood, but nobody has ported them to autos.
revenue_model: Flat fee (about $500-$700) or 3-5% of sale price per completed sale, plus a performance share of recovery improvement over projected repo loss.
non_obvious_insight: Lenders already lose money on repossession, but their servicing, collections and legal workflows are built around it, so no infrastructure exists to choreograph title, payoff and buyer across 50 states. The product is that plumbing.
first_30_days: Partner with two or three credit unions with 5k-plus delinquent auto loans. Run a manual pilot in one state with a small dealer buyer network, comparing net recovery per unit against actual auction results. Use the data to sign a master services agreement.

title: Disaster-Pause Rider for Small-Business Loans
one_liner: A parametric portfolio rider that lets CDFIs and credit unions automatically pause small-business and farm loan payments after a disaster, with the lender made whole by a pre-funded payout.
customer: Community lenders (CDFIs, credit unions, farm-credit and small-bank lenders) with $50-$500M loan books in disaster-exposed counties. The end beneficiaries are their small-business and consumer borrowers.
problem: After a hurricane, flood or fire, borrowers need a payment holiday, but lenders cannot afford to grant them automatically because the missed cash flow strains liquidity and reserves. Borrowers must plead, forbearance takes weeks of staff time, and many quietly default. CDFI funding is already fragile, so lenders hold back.
solution: A portfolio-level parametric policy keyed to county-level disaster declarations plus hazard footprints (wind swaths, flood extent, fire perimeters). It pays the lender the scheduled payments of borrowers in the footprint for 90-180 days. The loan documents carry a pre-approved 'automatic pause' clause, so borrowers never buy insurance. The lender markets 'storm-proof loans' and adds a rate rider of about 10-25 bps to pay for it. A software pause engine flags affected loans and sends notices.
why_now: Repeated large disasters and ongoing debate over shrinking or slowing federal disaster aid make private, fast liquidity more attractive. Federal support for CDFIs has been unsettled, so lenders want to protect portfolios. Parametric capacity is abundant and hazard-footprint data (NOAA swaths, flood extents) is public and precise.
revenue_model: MGA/brokerage fee of 15-20% on premium (roughly 25-60 bps of covered balance per year), plus a SaaS fee of $1,000-$5,000 per month for the pause-and-notice engine. Later, reinsurance placement and a data product on borrower resilience.
non_obvious_insight: After a disaster the scarce resource is lender liquidity, not rebuilding capital. A forbearance favor becomes a contractual right that costs the lender one clause, and distribution is the loan itself, so no borrower ever has to shop for or understand insurance.
first_30_days: Approach three Gulf Coast, Carolinas or California CDFIs and credit unions through CDFI trade networks. Write a one-page term sheet, price it from historical hazard footprints, and pilot on newly originated loans in one county. Pair with an MGA and a reinsurer, and target one signed letter of intent within 60 days.

title: Family Continuity Kit for Mixed-Status Households
one_liner: A done-with-you, notarized emergency-care package (standby guardianship, power of attorney, school and medical authorizations, wallet card and check-in alerts) for parents who could be detained without notice.
customer: Immigrant parents in mixed-status families, reached through trusted messengers such as churches, consulates, unions, clinics and schools. Co-payers: cities, counties and foundations funding preparedness, and employers in agriculture, meatpacking and hospitality. Price $49 to $149 per family, sliding scale.
problem: ICE issued Directive 11064.4 in July 2025 telling officers not to unnecessarily infringe parents' rights, but children still land in limbo when a parent is detained. The legal tools (standby guardianship, power of attorney, medical consent) are known, and nonprofits such as CLINIC and ILRC publish free guides. Execution is the bottleneck: state-specific forms, two-parent signatures, witnesses, a notary, and getting copies to the right person. California updated its guardianship rules in 2026, and city offices such as Chicago's 40th Ward publish emergency-plan guidance, which shows demand.
solution: A Spanish-first, WhatsApp-friendly workflow that interviews the parent, auto-fills the state's forms, and completes them through remote online notarization or notary-and-witness events at churches and clinics. Each family gets a wallet card with a QR code giving the designated caregiver instant access to the documents, plus school, bank and medical authorizations. Optional check-in alerts notify the caregiver and a legal-aid hotline if a parent misses a check-in. A caregiver checklist explains the first 72 hours. The forms are reviewed by legal-aid partners, and the app never collects immigration status.
why_now: Enforcement is at historically high levels in 2025 to 2026, and local governments are publishing family preparedness plans and updating guardianship law. Remote online notarization is available in most states, and messaging-app workflows reach families where they already are. Municipal and foundation budgets for know-your-rights work exist now.
revenue_model: $49 to $149 per family on a sliding scale. Municipal and county contracts to buy kits for residents ($25 to $40 each). Foundation grants. Union or employer benefit at about $5 per employee per year. Licensing to legal-aid organizations that lack completion capacity.
non_obvious_insight: For many immigrant families the highest-consequence legal document is not about immigration at all. It is a twenty-minute notarized form that keeps a child out of the foster system. Free guides exist but completion is low because the burden is witnesses, notaries, state variations and sharing, which can be productized. Payers exist beyond the family, since cities and foundations would rather fund kits than emergency foster placements.
first_30_days: Pick one state with a clear standby-guardianship statute. Have a legal-aid organization review the forms to avoid unauthorized-practice-of-law problems. Run notary-and-witness events at three churches or clinics and measure cost per completed family. Build the Spanish WhatsApp flow and printed wallet card, and design privacy so nothing about status is stored. Pitch one alderman's or county commissioner's office for a paid pilot of 500 kits.

title: Sub-Tier Surge Twin for the Industrial Base
one_liner: A digital twin of foundries, forges and motor makers that shows which supplier breaks first in a 180-day fight.
customer: Defense primes' supply-chain risk teams, private equity funds rolling up defense suppliers, DoD industrial-base offices, and sub-tier lenders.
problem: Leaders doubt they can sustain the 90-, 120- or 180-day fight and lack integrated supply-chain visibility. AIA-Bain identifies castings, forgings, sensors, semiconductors and solid rocket motors as bottlenecks. Private equity invests only $1-3B a year and is flying blind on capacity.
solution: Build a network model of sub-tier capacity from public and commercial data (facility permits, trade flows, workforce, energy use, certifications), calibrated by supplier surveys. Run agent-based surge scenarios to identify chokepoints and invest-or-acquire targets. Start with one commodity, castings and forgings.
why_now: The record defense funding wave is looking for bottlenecks to fund. Maven-scale AI targeting has raised concern about munition depth. Agentic simulation and cheap data enrichment make a 5-person twin feasible.
revenue_model: $60-250K per year per subscribing prime or fund, plus deal-sourcing fees on roll-up acquisitions.
non_obvious_insight: The people who will pay first are private equity funds hunting acquisition targets, not the Pentagon. The twin's early output is a target list for whoever wants to roll up the base.
first_30_days: Map 300 casting and forging plants from public data and publish a bottleneck brief. Present to 5 PE funds and 3 primes' supply-chain teams. Sign one paid pilot for a commodity view.

title: Buildings-as-Mines Salvage Reserve Reports
one_liner: Mining-style reserve estimates for buildings before demolition, built from phone LiDAR and AI that reads the drawings, then a market for pre-sold salvage rights.
customer: Demolition and selective-strip contractors and developers doing office-to-residential conversions (first), later scrap buyers, banks and salvors.
problem: Demolition bids depend on a walk-through guess of salvage value in copper, aluminum, steel, glass and fixtures. Contractors overpay or underbid, and no one sells forward the metals inside a building, unlike any mined commodity.
solution: A 48-hour reserve report with tonnage, value and confidence bands (P10/P50/P90). It uses LiDAR and thermal scans, stud and cable finders, and an LLM that reads as-builts and MEP drawings. A bid-day marketplace lets salvage buyers commit. Long term, salvage-rights forwards on the building stock.
why_now: Phone LiDAR and models that can read drawings became good enough in 2025-26, at a time when office conversions are surging and metal prices are elevated.
revenue_model: $1.5-5K per report, plus 3-5% of salvage value transacted through the marketplace.
non_obvious_insight: Demolition is the only mining-like business with no reserve estimate. Once a reserve report exists, salvage rights become financeable and pre-sellable.
first_30_days: Scan 10 buildings free with a partner contractor, then back-test estimates against actual scale tickets. Sell the first reports at $1,500 to 5 contractors.
